newsitem.title: MEXICO: Left-winger poised for landslide win in Mexico City.
newsitem.headline: Left-winger poised for landslide win in Mexico City.

text.p: A left-wing opposition leader was set to win the first election of mayor of this huge city, inflicting a crushing defeat on Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), an exit poll showed on Sunday.
In another big upset, President Ernesto Zedillo's party was also set to lose its majority in the lower house of congress for the first time, television polls said.
The PRI has won every presidential race and controlled both houses of Congress ever since it was founded in 1929.

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, a former governor who broke with the PRI in 1987 to form his own party, won 45.77 percent of the vote for mayor of Mexico City, nearly twice as much as his nearest rivals from the PRI, an exit poll by Indemerc/Louis Harris showed.
A beaming Cardenas appeared at the headquarters of his party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) making victory signs to supporters shortly after the exit poll was published.
"I hope that these figures are confirmed when we have the results," he said to shouts of "Cuauhtemoc, Cuauhtemoc". Preliminary official results were expected later on Sunday night.

Exit polls in the big northern industrial state of Nuevo Leon, where the PRI had claimed it was running neck and neck with the opposition, showed the PRI losing the governorship by a big margin to the right-wing National Action Party (PAN).
Most of the 52 million registered voters cast their ballots across the country in peace, though isolated incidents of irregularities were reported at some of the 104,700 polling stations.
The worst problems came in the southern state of Chiapas, where mobs of angry Indians burned or destroyed dozens of polling booths and blocked roads.

Zapatista chief Subcommander Marcos said last week Indians in southern Mexico would not participate in the elections as "a protest against militarization and the atmosphere of civil war promoted by federal and local governments."

Apparently unaware of the violence, President Ernesto Zedillo cast his ballot early in a school near the presidential palace. Hobbling on crutches after a minor knee operation, he told reporters: "I think voting is plentiful and I believe enthusiastic...Democracy speaks for itself. It has its own language, which is very beautiful."
All over the country, though, Mexicans appeared to be voting for change, either for the left-wing PRD or the right-wing PAN.

"I prefer Cardenas. He can change the one-party system we have because he knows the system from the inside," said Eduardo Rios, a 67-year-old retired schoolteacher voting in Mexico City's southern Coyoacan district.

Industrial engineer Antonio Cruz, 35, said he chose the PAN. "The PRI is a party that cannot be believed, there have been untold amounts of money stolen and they have achieved nothing for the country," he said.

The sale of alcoholic drinks was banned from midnight on Friday and tens of thousands of police officers were on duty to guarantee security for the election, billed by officials as the cleanest yet in a country with a history of polling fraud.
Jose Woldenberg, president of the newly independent Federal Electoral Institute (IFE), which is running the vote, pledged a clean election.

"As president of the Federal Electoral Institute, I want to reaffirm now the central commitment of this institution: every vote cast today will be rigorously respected," he said in a speech at the start of the election.

Political reforms pushed through by Zedillo last year included holding elections for mayor of Mexico City's Federal District -- a post previously filled by a presidential nominee -- and providing generous public funding for all political parties, including the opposition.

The Federal District is home to 8.5 million people, about half the population of the sprawling Mexico City metropolitan area. It also houses the federal government. The remainder of the Mexico City population lives in the state of Mexico, which has a different government.
The loss of a PRI majority in the lower house would have profound implications in a country where Congress has traditionally acted as a rubber stamp for the almost imperial will of the PRI president.
Voters will also choose a quarter of the Senate, but the PRI's majority there is so big it is not threatened.
